PARIS (AP) — Wilting in the summer sun, a line of tourists waits to climb [Notre Dame cathedral](https://apnews.com/article/1ddf4e7d38db44cb814f3672123db2a9) and meet its gargoyles. 巴黎（美联电）——一群游客在夏日的烈日下无精打采地排着队，等着攀登 [巴黎圣母院大教堂](https://apnews.com/article/1ddf4e7d38db44cb814f3672123db2a9) ，去见见那些滴水嘴兽。

Four meters (13 feet) beneath them, a team of archaeologists is digging the other way — straight down and back in time, to Roman Paris 2,000 years ago. 在他们下方四米（十三英尺）处，一队考古学家正朝着相反的方向挖掘——垂直向下，追溯至两千年前的罗马巴黎时期。

In 2019, fire brought Notre Dame’s spire crashing down as the world watched. The [cathedral was rebuilt](https://apnews.com/article/paris-notre-dame-macron-fire-reconstruction-0a6c183693b55a55e0dc3a909000cb02) and [reopened in late 2024](https://apnews.com/article/france-notre-dame-reopening-paris-macron-f2543dc70b4d89b256cde9aa53bbbd44), and now Paris wants to soften the hot, bare square in front of it with trees and shade.2019年，在全世界的注视下，一场大火让巴黎圣母院的尖顶轰然倒塌。 [这座大教堂完成了重建](https://apnews.com/article/paris-notre-dame-macron-fire-reconstruction-0a6c183693b55a55e0dc3a909000cb02) ，并于 [2024年末重新开放](https://apnews.com/article/france-notre-dame-reopening-paris-macron-f2543dc70b4d89b256cde9aa53bbbd44) ，如今巴黎希望用树木和遮荫来软化教堂前那片炙热、空旷的广场。

But in a city this old, the soil cannot be turned until what lies beneath it is excavated, in case it is damaged during works.但在这样一座古老的城市，翻土之前必须先挖掘出其下方的土层，以防施工过程中造成损坏。

So a slice of Notre Dame’s forecourt has become an excavation site — an open pit ringed by barriers and crossed by a wooden walkway, a few steps from the line-up.于是巴黎圣母院前院的一角变成了考古现场——一个被围栏环绕、设有木质走道的露天深坑，距离排队区只有几步之遥。

## A modern Da Vinci Code 现代版《达·芬奇密码》

French media have dubbed it the “dig of the century.” 法国媒体将其称作“世纪大发掘”。

“It’s a rare opportunity for us to work on something that’s tangibly going to make a difference to the history of Paris,” Lucie Altenburg, a conservator with the Paris archaeology unit, told The Associated Press.“能参与到这件切实为巴黎历史带来改变的工作，对我们来说是难得的机会。”巴黎考古部门的文物保护员吕西·阿尔滕堡告诉美联社。

Among the hundreds of objects already found: a fourth-century coin stamped with the face of the Emperor Constantine, and shards of medieval pottery painted on the inside with marks no expert has yet deciphered — like a modern Da Vinci Code.在已发现的数百件文物中，有一枚刻有君士坦丁大帝头像的四世纪硬币，还有内部绘有专家至今仍未破译符号的中世纪陶器碎片——宛如现代版的《达·芬奇密码》。

“It makes Notre Dame feel alive again,” said Emily Carter, 34, a tourist from Manchester waiting in line with her two children. “You come to see the cathedral, then realize there’s another city under your feet. That’s almost more moving.” “这让巴黎圣母院重新焕发生机，”34岁的艾米丽·卡特说，她是来自曼彻斯特的游客，正带着两个孩子排队。“你来看这座大教堂，却会发现脚下还有另一座城市。这种感觉甚至更令人动容。”

The first traces appear 50 centimeters (20 inches) down; 4 meters (13 feet) lower, the team is still pulling up the past. Some days they fill 15 crates — from ground that has lain untouched for decades.最初的痕迹出现在地下50厘米（20英寸）处；再往下4米（13英尺），团队仍在挖掘过去。有些日子，他们能从这片尘封数十年的土地上挖出15个箱子。

## Ancient cities have archaeologists monitoring digs古城有考古学家监守发掘现场

This is the bargain in every old city: The past is not in a museum down the street — it is under the street.每一座老城都有这样的约定：过去不在街边的博物馆里——它就在街道之下。

Cities rise. Each age builds on the rubble of the last, and the ground climbs with it; in Rome, it has risen about 9 meters (30 feet) since the empire fell in the fifth century AD.城市拔地而起。每个时代都在前代的废墟之上重建，地面也随之抬升；在罗马，自公元5世纪帝国覆灭以来，地面已抬升了约9米（30英尺）。

When Athens built its metro for the 2004 Olympics, it set off the largest excavation in Greek history and turned up tens of thousands of objects, now shown in the stations themselves. Paris is no different. 雅典为2004年奥运会修建地铁时，开展了希腊历史上规模最大的考古发掘工作，出土了数万件文物，如今这些文物就陈列在地铁各站点中。巴黎的情况也大同小异。

It all comes from the island in the Seine, the Ile de la Cite, where Paris began. 这一切都来自塞纳河上的西岱岛，巴黎便是从这里发端的。

Centuries later, Notre Dame rose on the same ground.几个世纪后，巴黎圣母院就建在了同一片土地上。

At the cathedral’s birth in 1163, the entire square was packed with medieval houses, split by a single street, said Camille Colonna, the archaeologist leading the dig. 主持此次发掘工作的考古学家卡米耶·科隆纳表示，1163年大教堂初建时，整个广场上挤满了中世纪房屋，中间仅隔着一条街道。

Digging down, her team has reached their cellars — and therefore also the time in history they represent. 深入挖掘后，她的团队已经抵达了这些地窖——也因此触碰到了它们所代表的那段历史时期。

Below them lie Merovingian and Carolingian grain pits, from the sixth to the 10th centuries; below those, darker and deeper still, a dense Roman quarter from the fourth and fifth centuries.其下方是公元6至10世纪的墨洛温王朝和加洛林王朝谷仓坑；再往下，颜色更深、位置更深处，是公元4至5世纪的密集罗马街区遗迹。

Twenty centuries are stacked in 4 meters (13 feet) of earth — or about the height of two-and-a-half Napoleon Bonapartes standing on top of one another. 四米厚的土层中堆叠着二十个世纪——大约相当于两个半拿破仑·波拿巴叠在一起的高度。

“Here you can see the layers — medieval Paris, Roman Paris, maybe even before that,” said Yasmine Benali, 22, an archaeology student watching from behind the barriers. “It makes the city feel less like a postcard and more like something still being discovered.” “在这里你能看到这些地层——中世纪的巴黎、罗马时期的巴黎，甚至可能更早，”22岁的考古学学生雅斯敏·贝纳利站在围栏后说道，“这让这座城市不再像一张明信片，而更像是一个仍有待发掘的存在。”

## Coins, ceramics and mysterious markings硬币、陶瓷与神秘印记

The richest finds here come from the foulest place: the deep pits beneath the medieval houses, old latrines that doubled as rubbish dumps. 这里最珍贵的发现来自最污秽的地方：中世纪房屋下方的深坑，以及曾兼作垃圾场的古老厕所。

Out of them the team keeps lifting whole jugs and cups — thrown away centuries ago, yet still intact — among the broken plates and animal bones.在这些碎片中，团队不断搬出完整的罐子和杯子——它们是几个世纪前被丢弃的，却依然完好无损——混杂在破碎的盘子和动物骨骼之中。

It’s “rare to find complete ceramics,” said Valentine Breloux, an archaeologist with the unit.该团队的考古学家瓦伦丁·布雷卢说：“很难找到完整的陶瓷器。”

Here the soft waste cushioned them, and centuries later they miraculously came up whole.这里松软的废弃物起到了缓冲作用，数百年后它们奇迹般地完整出土。

Then some other objects came that confounded experts. As conservators cleaned what looked like ordinary medieval pottery, they found faint reddish writing painted on the inside — the same mysterious markings on shard after shard. 随后出现了一些让专家们困惑不已的其他器物。文物保护人员清理那些看似普通的中世纪陶器时，发现内壁上绘有淡淡的红色文字——每一块碎片上都有着同样神秘的标记。

What they mean has yet to be deciphered. 它们的含义还有待破译。

Of everything she has cleaned from Notre Dame, Breloux said, these are the most “astonishing.” 布雷卢说，在她从巴黎圣母院清理出的所有物品中，这些是最“令人惊叹”的。

## Coins can help date the layers 硬币有助于确定地层年代

The coins came up as black discs, eaten by rust. But under an X-ray, a face returned: it was Constantine, the Roman emperor who ruled in the early 300s AD.这些硬币变成了被锈蚀吞噬的黑色圆片。但在X光下，一张面容重现了：那是君士坦丁，公元4世纪初统治罗马的皇帝。

Such objects also “can be invaluable in giving us the date of the (underground) layer,” Altenburg said.阿尔滕堡表示，这类物体“在为我们确定（地下）地层的年代方面也可能具有极高的价值”。

The Roman finds are the ones the archaeologists value most — the deepest, oldest and least understood. In Roman times, the town was called Lutetia, and its center lay across the river, on the Left Bank. 罗马时期的遗迹是考古学家们最珍视的发现——它们年代最久远、埋藏最深，也最不为人知。在罗马时代，这座城镇被称为卢泰西亚，其中心位于河对岸的左岸。

As the Roman empire collapsed, people pulled back to the Ile de la Cite, where Notre Dame would later rise, and fortified the island with walls of stone taken from earlier buildings.随着罗马帝国崩溃，人们退至西岱岛，巴黎圣母院后来便矗立于此；他们用从早期建筑中拆取的石材为这座岛屿修筑了城墙。

Colonna’s team found some proof: a Roman doorstep found in the dig, taken from a much bigger building, carried over, turned upside down, and laid in a road as paving.科洛纳的团队发现了一些证据：在挖掘现场出土的一块罗马门阶，原本来自一座更大的建筑，被搬运过来后倒放在路上当作铺路石。

## Paris houses thousands of finds in an archaeology center巴黎有一座考古中心，收藏着数千件出土文物

Every find leaves the pit and travels north, to the city’s archaeology center — what Colonna calls “a huge archaeological store,” a treasure house of Paris.每一次发掘都让深坑向北延伸，直达城市的考古中心——科洛纳称之为“一座巨大的考古宝库”，巴黎的宝藏库。

For archaeologists, the cathedral dig is a rare treat. In France, like elsewhere, they work only where building work is about to begin — a bit like how industrial quarry workers end up unearthing dinosaur remains. 对考古学家来说，这座大教堂的发掘工作是难得的乐事。和其他地方一样，在法国，他们只在即将开工的建筑区域开展工作——这有点像工业采石场的工人偶然发掘出恐龙化石。

“This only happens because the city of Paris decided it wanted to beautify the area,” Altenburg said.“这一切的发生只是因为巴黎市想要美化这片区域，”阿尔滕堡说。

The [new square](https://apnews.com/article/france-paris-notre-dame-green-ecology-2b1930e4630e48994a6bd758a747ebbc) should be mostly finished by 2028: a kind of woodland clearing, with 160 new trees and a thin film of water sliding over the stone to cool it in summer — part of how Paris is bracing for ever hotter summers induced by global warming.[新广场](https://apnews.com/article/france-paris-notre-dame-green-ecology-2b1930e4630e48994a6bd758a747ebbc) 预计将于2028年基本完工：这是一片林地空地，将种植160棵新树，还会有一层薄薄的水流过石板，在夏季为石板降温——这是巴黎为应对全球变暖导致的持续高温夏季所做的准备工作之一。

The tourists who now wait in the bare sun beneath the gargoyles will, in a few summers, line up in the shade.如今在滴水兽下方光秃秃的阳光下排队等候的游客们，再过几个夏天，就会在阴凉处排起长队。

The old underground parking lot will reopen as a visitor center looking onto the Seine. 这座老旧的地下停车场将重新开放，作为一座可俯瞰塞纳河的游客中心。

Until then, the Notre Dame team wants to go deeper still — past the Romans, toward whoever came before them, the Gauls who gave the city its first name.在那之前，巴黎圣母院团队还想进一步追溯——越过罗马人，去探寻更早的先民，也就是为这座城市定下最初名字的高卢人。

“The hope is that we are able to go back in time even further than we’ve ever been before,” Altenburg said.“我们希望能比以往任何时候都追溯到更久远的过去，”阿尔滕堡说。

\_\_\_

Nicolas Garriga in Paris contributed.尼古拉斯·加里加发自巴黎报道。
